title: Back of envelope estimation drills
story:
This lesson is practice rather than exposition, but it needs one correction before the drills, because the usual way these figures are taught produces confident wrongness.

The table everyone memorises comes from the 2009 keynote: a first-level cache reference around half a nanosecond, a main memory reference around a hundred, sending two kilobytes over a gigabit network around twenty thousand, a datacenter round trip around five hundred thousand, a disk seek around ten million, a megabyte read sequentially from disk around thirty million.

Those numbers are stale, and predictably so. An interactive update of them exists precisely because somebody noticed a real-world latency figure was an order of magnitude smaller than the memorised one, hardware performance increasing exponentially — and there is a plausible claim that the table's provenance predates that keynote anyway. So memorising the values is the wrong move. What survives is the ratios and the method: memory is about a hundred times a cache reference, a datacenter round trip is about five thousand memory references, a disk seek is about twenty datacenter round trips. Those drift more slowly than the absolutes, and they are what the decisions actually turn on.

The third tool is the queuing relationship, which is unusually well suited to estimation because it assumes almost nothing: items in the system equals arrival rate times time in system, independently of the arrival distribution, the service distribution and the service order. You can use it without knowing anything about the workload's shape, which is exactly the situation you are in when estimating.

Now the drills. Each should take two minutes, be done aloud, and end in a number with one significant figure.

How much storage does a year of events take at ten thousand per second? Rate times seconds per year times bytes per event, then times replication. How many machines serve a million requests per second at fifty milliseconds each? Concurrency is arrival rate times duration, then divide by concurrency per machine. Does a hundred million user records fit in memory on one machine? Count times bytes each, compare against a number you know. How long to transfer a terabyte across a network you know the bandwidth of? Size over rate, and notice the answer is in hours. What does it cost to embed a million documents, and is that a batch job or an interactive one? Count times cost per call, then look at the total and let it tell you which.

The discipline in all five: write the assumptions beside the answer, and say which one you are least sure of. That sentence is what turns an estimate into something another person can check rather than believe.

problem.name: Estimation practice
problem.shape: A decision requires a quantity nobody has measured, and the alternatives differ by orders of magnitude.
tell: a proposal has no numbers attached
two designs are compared by which sounds faster
nobody can say whether something fits on one machine
an estimate uses remembered constants of unknown age
problem.move: Work aloud to one significant figure using ratios rather than values. Storage is count times size times replication; concurrency is arrival rate times duration including waiting; transfer time is size over bandwidth. Write the assumptions beside the answer and name the one you are least sure of.
problem.invariant: The ratios between levels of the hierarchy drift far more slowly than the absolute latencies, so a method built on relationships survives hardware improvement while memorised constants do not.
problem.breaks: The constants are stale and were probably stale when you learned them — an interactive update exists because a real figure turned out an order of magnitude below the memorised one, and the table's provenance may predate the talk it is attributed to. An estimate is only as current as its inputs, and nothing announces when they expire.

cost.time: two minutes, against a build that may go months in the wrong direction
cost.beats: benchmarking, which requires the thing to exist, and intuition, which is systematically wrong in a known direction about the network and disk

worked.problem: How would you estimate whether a design fits on one machine?
worked.reasoning:
By establishing what one machine has, estimating what the design needs in the same units, and comparing to one significant figure. The whole exercise should take two minutes and end in a number you would be willing to say aloud.

Start by deciding which resource binds, because fits on one machine is three different questions. Memory: does the working set fit. Storage: does the data fit. Throughput: can one machine serve the rate. They have different arithmetic and a design can pass two and fail the third.

For memory, the arithmetic is count times bytes each. A hundred million user records at a hundred bytes each is ten gigabytes, which fits comfortably; at a kilobyte each it is a hundred gigabytes, which is a large but real machine; at ten kilobytes it is a terabyte and the answer is no. Notice the decision changed twice on an assumption about record size, which is why that assumption is the one to state.

For throughput, use the queuing relationship, because it assumes almost nothing: items in the system equals arrival rate times time in system, independently of the arrival distribution, the service distribution and the service order. A million requests per second at fifty milliseconds each means fifty thousand concurrent, and the question becomes whether one machine can hold fifty thousand in flight — which for threads is no and for asynchronous handlers is arguable. The trap is using service time rather than time in system, because waiting counts and is usually the larger part.

For storage, count times size times replication, and the replication factor is the one people drop. What you buy is not what you store.

Then the check that saves you from the most common error, which is an instinct rather than an arithmetic mistake. If the design involves reading from another machine, remember that a datacenter round trip is around five hundred thousand nanoseconds while a disk seek is around ten million — so writes to the network within a datacenter are much faster than writes to local disk. People estimating from a feeling that the network is slow get the comparison backwards, and that feeling is correct across the internet and wrong inside a building.

The caution I would state explicitly is about the constants rather than the method. They are stale and predictably so — an interactive update of the figures exists because somebody noticed a real latency was an order of magnitude below the memorised value, hardware improving exponentially, and the table's provenance may predate the talk it is attributed to. So I hold the ratios rather than the values: memory is about a hundred cache references, a datacenter round trip about five thousand memory references, a disk seek about twenty round trips. Those drift much more slowly.

And the part that makes an estimate useful to somebody else: write the assumptions next to the answer, and say which one you are least sure of. That converts a number to be believed or dismissed into a claim that can be checked.

problem.practice: Do all five drills aloud in ten minutes without looking anything up, writing the assumptions beside each answer. Then look up the two figures you were least sure of and see how far off you were — that gap is what the ratios are for.

beats.broke: You have to choose between designs before either exists, and the choice turns on quantities nobody has measured because the thing has not been built.
beats.fix: Estimate to an order of magnitude using a handful of remembered ratios and arithmetic you can do aloud, because the decision usually turns on whether a number is thousands or billions rather than on its exact value.
beats.cost: The remembered figures go stale at different rates, so the method outlives the constants and anyone who memorised the constants without the method will be confidently wrong.

interview.q: How would you estimate whether a design fits on one machine?
interview.trap: Answering before deciding which resource binds. Fits on one machine is three questions — memory, storage and throughput — and a design can pass two and fail the third, so the estimate starts by naming which one is being asked.
interview.answer:
By establishing what one machine has, estimating what the design needs in the same units, and comparing to one significant figure — two minutes, ending in a number I would say aloud.
